tanagra-figurine.s: Tanagra figurines are Greek terracotta statuettes, mostly of elegantly dressed women, made from the later 4th century BCE and named after Tanagra in Boeotia, where many were found in tombs in the 1870s. Cast in moulds and painted, they show ordinary people rather than gods.

tanganyika-african-national-union.s: The Tanganyika African National Union (TANU) was the nationalist party that led Tanganyika to independence in 1961. Founded by Julius Nyerere in 1954, it won the elections of 1958–1960 and became the sole legal party on the mainland in 1965.

taranchi.s: The Taranchi were the Uyghur farmers of the Ili valley in northern Xinjiang, descended from people of the Tarim basin oases moved there by the Dzungars and later the Qing to grow grain. In 1864 they rose against the Qing and formed a sultanate at Ghulja, which Russia occupied…

tarcondimotus-i.s: Tarcondimotus I (died 31 BCE) was the ruler of a client kingdom in the Amanus mountains of eastern Cilicia, recognised by Pompey in 64 BCE. Ruling from Hierapolis-Castabala, he supported the Roman commanders of the East in turn, took the surname Philantonios ('friend of…

tages.s: Tages was a figure of Etruscan religion, a child with the wisdom of an old man who, according to legend, sprang from a ploughed furrow near Tarquinii. He was said to have revealed the Etruscan discipline of divination, including the reading of entrails by haruspices, to the…

tarchon.s: Tarchon was a legendary Etruscan hero, said in ancient tradition to have founded Tarquinii and other cities of Etruria. Some versions make him the brother or son of Tyrrhenus, who led the Etruscans from Lydia, and in Virgil's Aeneid he commands the Etruscans as an ally of Aeneas.

tarquinius-priscus.s: Lucius Tarquinius Priscus was, according to Roman tradition, the fifth king of Rome, reigning from 616 to 579 BCE. Said to be the son of Demaratus, a Corinthian exile who settled at Tarquinii, he moved to Rome and won the throne after the death of Ancus Marcius.

tugu-inscription.s: The Tugu inscription is a 5th-century Sanskrit inscription of King Purnawarman of Tarumanagara, found at Tugu in North Jakarta, Indonesia. It records the digging of the Gomati canal, more than 11 kilometres long, in 21 days, and a gift of 1,000 cattle to Brahmins on its…

teuta.s: Teuta was queen of the Ardiaean kingdom of Illyria, ruling as regent for her stepson Pinnes after the death of her husband Agron in 231 BCE. Illyrian raids on Greek cities and Italian traders under her rule, and the killing of a Roman envoy, provoked the First Illyrian War in…

timaeus-of-tauromenium.s: Timaeus of Tauromenium was a Greek historian from Sicily, the son of the city's founder Andromachus. Exiled by the tyrant Agathocles, he spent about fifty years in Athens, where he wrote a long history of Sicily and the western Greeks down to 264 BCE.

tecumseh.s: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native American peoples to resist the expansion of the United States into the Old Northwest. With his brother Tenskwatawa he founded Prophetstown in 1808 and rejected land cessions such as the Treaty of Fort Wayne.

tenskwatawa.s: Tenskwatawa, known as the Shawnee Prophet, was a Shawnee religious leader and the brother of Tecumseh. After a vision in 1805 he preached the rejection of alcohol and American goods and a return to Native ways, inspiring a movement across many nations.

tippecanoe-river.s: The Tippecanoe River is a river of northern Indiana, flowing nearly 300 kilometres south-west to join the Wabash River above Lafayette. Prophetstown stood near the confluence, and the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811 took its name from the river.

treaty-of-fort-wayne-1809.s: The Treaty of Fort Wayne of 30 September 1809 was signed between William Henry Harrison, governor of Indiana Territory, and leaders of the Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami and Eel River peoples. It ceded about three million acres of land in present-day Indiana and Illinois to the…

tilari-massacre.s: The Tilari massacre took place on 30 May 1930 at Tilari, in the Rawain area of Tehri Garhwal State in the Himalaya, when the state's troops fired on villagers gathered to protest new forest rules that restricted their customary rights. Many were killed or drowned in the Yamuna…

terengganu-inscription-stone.s: The Terengganu Inscription Stone is a granite stone found at Kuala Berang in Terengganu, Malaysia, bearing a text in Malay written in Jawi script. Dated to the early 14th century, probably 1303, it sets out Islamic laws issued by a local ruler and is the oldest known evidence…

tok-pisin.s: Tok Pisin is an English-based creole language spoken across Papua New Guinea and one of its official languages. It grew from the pidgin used on plantations in Samoa, Queensland and New Guinea in the 19th century, with words also drawn from German, Malay and local languages.

tiberias.s: Tiberias is a city on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee in northern Israel. Founded by Herod Antipas around 19 CE and named after the emperor Tiberius, it became his capital and later a leading centre of Jewish scholarship, where much of the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled.

trachonitis.s: Trachonitis was a rugged lava field south of Damascus, in present-day Syria, now known as the Lajat. Its caves sheltered brigands, and Augustus gave it to Herod the Great in the 20s BCE to suppress them.

texcotzinco.s: Texcotzinco is an archaeological site on a hill east of Texcoco, in the State of Mexico, built in the 15th century as a retreat and garden by the Acolhua ruler Nezahualcoyotl. Water was brought by aqueduct to baths, fountains and terraced gardens cut into the rock, with…

toxandria.s: Toxandria was a region of the late Roman Empire between the Meuse and the Scheldt, in the present-day Campine of Belgium and the Netherlands, named after the Texuandri people. Salian Franks settled there in the 4th century, and in 358 the Caesar Julian accepted their…

thembu.s: The Thembu are a Xhosa-speaking Nguni people of the Eastern Cape, South Africa, whose homeland, Thembuland, lies around the Mbashe and Mthatha rivers. Their paramount king held senior rank among the southern Nguni royal houses.

timok.s: The Timok is a river of the eastern Balkans that rises in eastern Serbia and flows north into the Danube, forming part of the border between Serbia and Bulgaria in its lower course. Its valley was settled by Slavs in the 7th century, among them the Timočani, and was contested…

tetlepanquetzal.s: Tetlepanquetzal was the last independent tlatoani of Tlacopan, the third member of the Aztec Triple Alliance. He fought the Spanish alongside Cuauhtemoc during the siege of Tenochtitlan in 1521, and after its fall he was tortured with Cuauhtemoc by conquistadors seeking…

toluca-valley.s: The Toluca Valley is a high basin in the State of Mexico, west of the Valley of Mexico, drained by the upper Lerma river and centred on the city of Toluca. Before the Spanish conquest it was home to Matlatzinca, Otomi and Mazahua peoples.

tepeticpac.s: Tepeticpac was the oldest of the four altepetl, or city-states, that formed the Nahua state of Tlaxcala in central Mexico, founded on a fortified hilltop by the first settlers in the 14th century. It ranked first among the four in tradition, alongside Ocotelolco, Quiahuixtlan…

tizatlan.s: Tizatlan was one of the four altepetl, or city-states, that formed the Nahua state of Tlaxcala in central Mexico. At the Spanish arrival in 1519 it was ruled by the elderly Xicotencatl, whose son Xicotencatl the Younger led the Tlaxcalan army against Cortés.

tokushima.s: Tokushima is a city on the east coast of Shikoku, Japan, at the mouth of the Yoshino river, and the capital of Tokushima Prefecture. It grew as the castle town of the Hachisuka lords, who built Tokushima Castle after receiving Awa province in 1585 and ruled from it until 1871.

tokushima-prefecture.s: Tokushima Prefecture is a prefecture of Japan in the east of Shikoku, corresponding to the former province of Awa, with its capital at Tokushima. It was created in 1871 when the Tokushima domain of the Hachisuka family was abolished, and after a period of merger with…

topiltzin-quetzalcoatl.s: Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, also called Ce Acatl from his birth date, was a priest-king of Tula remembered in later Aztec and other Mesoamerican traditions as the ideal ruler of the Toltecs. The stories say he opposed human sacrifice, was tricked into disgrace by the god…

tula-mesoamerican-site.s: Tula is an archaeological site in Hidalgo, central Mexico, the capital of the Toltecs, which flourished from about 900 to 1150 CE and may have held tens of thousands of people. Its ceremonial core, Tula Grande, includes Pyramid B with its colossal warrior columns, colonnaded…

tansen.s: Tansen was an Indian musician and composer, the most celebrated figure of Hindustani classical music. Trained in the dhrupad style that had grown up at the Tomara court of Gwalior, he served Raja Ramchandra of Rewa until about 1562, when he joined the court of the Mughal…

tansen-nepal.s: Tansen is a hill town in western Nepal, the headquarters of Palpa District, on a ridge of the Mahabharat range. From the 16th century it was the capital of the Sen kings of Palpa, once the strongest of the Chaubise Rajya, until its annexation by the Gorkha kingdom in 1806.

takechi-hanpeita.s: Takechi Hanpeita was a samurai and swordsman of the Tosa domain on Shikoku who in 1861 founded the Tosa Loyalist Party, dedicated to restoring imperial rule and expelling foreigners. His followers assassinated the domain's reforming minister Yoshida Toyo in 1862, and for a…

tottori.s: Tottori is a city on the Sea of Japan coast of western Honshu and the capital of Tottori Prefecture. Its castle on Mount Kyusho was the scene of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's siege of 1581, in which he starved the garrison into surrender.

tottori-prefecture.s: Tottori Prefecture is the least populous prefecture of Japan, on the Sea of Japan coast of western Honshu, with its capital at Tottori. It corresponds to the old provinces of Inaba and Hoki, which formed the Tottori domain of the Ikeda family until the abolition of the domains…

tijaniyya.s: The Tijaniyya is a Sufi order founded by the Algerian scholar Ahmad al-Tijani in the late 18th century and centred on Fez in Morocco. It spread widely in West Africa, where its claim of a direct spiritual link to the Prophet attracted scholars and rulers.

tui-lau.s: Tui Lau is a Fijian chiefly title meaning paramount chief of the Lau Islands in eastern Fiji. It was recognised for the Tongan noble Enele Maʻafu, the dominant power in Lau, when Fiji was ceded to Britain in 1874.

truc-lam-zen.s: Truc Lam Zen is a Vietnamese school of Zen Buddhism founded at the end of the 13th century by the retired emperor Tran Nhan Tong, who became a monk on Mount Yen Tu. It combined Chan meditation with Confucian and native traditions and is regarded as the first school of Buddhism…

transcaspian-oblast.s: The Transcaspian Oblast was a province of the Russian Empire east of the Caspian Sea, roughly corresponding to modern Turkmenistan, formed after the conquest of the Turkmen in 1881 and enlarged by the annexation of Merv in 1884. Its capital was Ashgabat, and the Trans-Caspian…

tigray-peoples-liberation-front.s: The Tigray People's Liberation Front is a political party and former guerrilla movement founded in 1975 in the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia. It led the armed struggle against the Derg and dominated the EPRDF coalition that took power in 1991, with its leader Meles Zenawi…

transvaal-province.s: The Transvaal Province was one of the four provinces of the Union of South Africa and later the Republic, formed in 1910 from the Transvaal Colony, the former South African Republic. It contained Pretoria, the administrative capital, and the gold-mining city of Johannesburg on…

temple-entry-proclamation.s: The Temple Entry Proclamation was issued on 12 November 1936 by Maharaja Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma of Travancore, ending the ban on entry of so-called lower castes and Dalits into the Hindu temples controlled by the state. Following years of campaigning such as the…

thiruvananthapuram.s: Thiruvananthapuram, formerly Trivandrum, is the capital of the Indian state of Kerala, near the southern tip of India. It grew around the Padmanabhaswamy Temple and became the capital of Travancore in the late 18th century, when the court moved there from Padmanabhapuram.

trebinje.s: Trebinje is a town in the south of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the Trebišnjica river close to Dubrovnik. In the early Middle Ages it was the centre of the Serb principality of Travunia, later passing to Serbia and then to Bosnia.

titus-labienus.s: Titus Labienus was a Roman general, Julius Caesar's most trusted legate in the Gallic Wars of 58–50 BCE. He defeated the Treveri in 53 BCE and the Parisii and their allies near Lutetia in 52 BCE.

titelberg.s: The Titelberg is a plateau in south-western Luxembourg, near Differdange, that held one of the largest oppida of the Treveri, a fortified Celtic town of about 40 hectares occupied from the 2nd century BCE. Excavations have found a mint, workshops, a public assembly area and…

troyes.s: Troyes is a city on the Seine in the Champagne region of north-eastern France. Founded under Augustus as Augustobona, the chief town of the Tricasses, it later took their name.

trinh-khai.s: Trinh Khai was the penultimate Trinh lord, ruling northern Vietnam in the name of the Le emperors from 1782 to 1786. He came to power through a mutiny of the palace troops against his half-brother, which left the soldiers dominant at court.

trinh-bong.s: Trinh Bong was the last of the Trinh lords who ruled northern Vietnam in the name of the Le emperors. He was installed in 1786 after the Tay Son had overthrown Trinh Khai, but the Le emperor Le Chieu Thong and his ally Nguyen Huu Chinh opposed him, and he fled Thang Long in…

treaty-of-ouchy.s: The Treaty of Ouchy, signed at Ouchy near Lausanne on 18 October 1912, ended the Italo-Turkish War. The Ottoman Empire withdrew its forces and officials from Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, which Italy had already annexed as Libya.

tripura.s: Tripura is a small state in north-eastern India, bordered on three sides by Bangladesh, with its capital at Agartala. For centuries it was a kingdom ruled by the Manikya dynasty, which contested Chittagong and the plains with Bengal, Arakan and the Mughals.

troezen-decree.s: The Troezen Decree is a marble inscription found at Troezen in 1959 and published by Michael Jameson in 1960. Carved in the 3rd century BCE, it claims to reproduce the decree proposed by Themistocles in 480 BCE ordering the evacuation of Athenian women and children to Troezen…

trucial-states-council.s: The Trucial States Council was a body set up by Britain in 1952 in which the rulers of the seven Trucial sheikhdoms met regularly under the chairmanship of the British Political Agent. It discussed common matters such as roads, health and education, and from 1965 it had its…

tanguts.s: The Tanguts were a people of north-western China, speaking a Tibeto-Burman language, who lived in the Ordos and the Gansu corridor. Under the Li clan they founded the Western Xia state, whose ruler Li Yuanhao declared himself emperor in 1038 and introduced a Tangut script in…

tsu-mie.s: Tsu is the capital of Mie Prefecture in central Japan, on the western shore of Ise Bay. Its medieval port was ruined by the earthquake of 1498, and it was refounded as a castle town by Tōdō Takatora after he received the domain in 1608.

tsushima-island.s: Tsushima is a mountainous island in the Korea Strait between Kyushu and the Korean peninsula, now part of Nagasaki Prefecture. Its rulers, the Sō clan, depended on trade with Korea and managed Japan's relations with the Joseon court, including the trading post at Busan.

tongatapu.s: Tongatapu is the main island of Tonga, in the southern part of the kingdom, and holds most of its people and the capital, Nukuʻalofa. A low coral island around a shallow lagoon, it was the seat of the Tuʻi Tonga kings, whose royal tombs stand at Lapaha near Muʻa, and it has…

tui-haatakalaua.s: The Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua was the second line of Tongan kings, created in the 15th century after the assassination of the Tuʻi Tonga Takalaua. His son Kauʻulufonua I avenged him and gave his brother Moʻungāmotuʻa authority over everyday government, while the Tuʻi Tonga kept sacred…

tuitatui.s: Tuʻitātui was a Tuʻi Tonga, sacred king of Tonga, who in tradition reigned around 1200. He is remembered as a powerful ruler who extended Tongan influence over neighbouring islands, and his name, 'king who strikes the knee', is linked to a story that he kept people at a…

tongeren.s: Tongeren is a town in the province of Limburg in eastern Belgium and claims to be the oldest town in the country. As Atuatuca Tungrorum it was founded under Augustus as the chief town of the Tungri and grew into a walled Roman city on the road from Bavay to Cologne.

turkestan-commission.s: The Turkestan Commission was a body sent by the Soviet government in Moscow to Tashkent in 1919 to take control of the Turkestan ASSR, which had been cut off during the civil war. Its members, including Mikhail Frunze and Valerian Kuibyshev, curbed the chauvinism of Russian…

trans-caspian-railway.s: The Trans-Caspian Railway was built by the Russian army from 1880, starting on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea, to supply the conquest of the Turkmen lands. Under General Mikhail Annenkov it reached Ashgabat in 1885, Merv in 1886 and Samarkand in 1888, and was extended to…

tours.s: Tours is a city on the Loire in west-central France and the historic capital of Touraine. Founded by the Romans as Caesarodunum, the chief town of the Turones, it became a great pilgrimage centre after the death of its bishop Saint Martin in 397.

tar-river.s: The Tar River flows south-east across the piedmont and coastal plain of North Carolina; below the town of Washington its estuary is called the Pamlico River, which opens into Pamlico Sound. Before European settlement its valley lay within the lands of the Tuscarora.

telegonus.s: Telegonus is a figure of Greek mythology, the son of Odysseus and the enchantress Circe. In the lost epic Telegony he sails to Ithaca in search of his father and kills him without recognising him, then takes Penelope and Telemachus back to Circe's island.

tusculan-disputations.s: The Tusculan Disputations is a philosophical work by Cicero in five books, written in 45 BCE and set at his country villa at Tusculum. Composed as dialogues after the death of his daughter Tullia, it discusses the fear of death, the endurance of pain, grief, the emotions and…

tuvan-peoples-revolutionary-party.s: The Tuvan People's Revolutionary Party was the ruling communist party of the Tuvan People's Republic, the Soviet-backed state in southern Siberia. From 1932 its leader Salchak Toka imposed a Stalinist regime, collectivising herds, closing Buddhist monasteries and persecuting…

tyana.s: Tyana was an ancient city of southern Cappadocia in central Anatolia, at modern Kemerhisar near Niğde. Known to the Hittites as Tuwanuwa, it was the capital of the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Tuwana in the 8th century BCE.

takelot-ii.s: Takelot II was a king of the Libyan period of Egypt in the second half of the 9th century BCE, usually placed in the Twenty-second Dynasty. His reign was troubled by civil war in Upper Egypt: his son, the Crown Prince Osorkon, served as High Priest of Amun and fought rebels in…

thebe-of-pherae.s: Thebe of Pherae was a daughter of Jason of Pherae and the wife of Alexander, tyrant of Pherae in Thessaly. Around 358 BCE she plotted with her brothers to murder her husband, whose cruelty was notorious; according to ancient writers she hid his guards' weapons and let her…

taibugids.s: The Taibugids were a dynasty of the Siberian Tatars who claimed descent from a legendary ruler named Taibuga. Around 1495 they seized power from the Shibanid khans of Tyumen and moved the capital to Qashliq on the Irtysh, founding the Khanate of Sibir.

tura-river.s: The Tura is a river of the Urals and western Siberia in Russia, flowing east from the Ural Mountains for over 1,000 kilometres to join the Tobol. The Tatar town of Chimgi-Tura, centre of the Tyumen Khanate, stood on its banks, and the Russians founded Tyumen on the site in 1586.

tzutujil-people.s: The Tz'utujil are a Maya people living around Lake Atitlán in the highlands of Guatemala. From the 13th century they formed a kingdom with its capital at Chuitinamit near present-day Santiago Atitlán, controlling the lake shores and cacao lands on the Pacific slope, and fought…

tevfik-esenc.s: Tevfik Esenç was a Turkish villager of Ubykh descent who became the last fluent speaker of the Ubykh language. Born in a Ubykh community resettled in Anatolia after the Circassian expulsions of 1864, he worked from the 1950s with linguists such as Georges Dumézil and later…

third-universal.s: The Third Universal of the Central Rada, issued in Kyiv on 20 November 1917 after the Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd, proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic. It declared the new republic part of a future federal Russia rather than independent, and announced land…

tyumen.s: Tyumen is a city in western Siberia, Russia, on the Tura river. It stands on the site of Chimgi-Tura, a seat of the Shibanid khans and the capital of the Tyumen Khanate in the 15th century.

tobol-river.s: The Tobol is a river of Kazakhstan and western Siberia, about 1,590 kilometres long, which rises in the southern Ural region and flows north to join the Irtysh at Tobolsk. Its basin lay within the appanage of Shiban in the Golden Horde and later within the Khanate of Sibir.

todi.s: Todi, the ancient Tuder, is a hill town above the Tiber valley in Umbria, central Italy. It was an Umbrian town on the border with Etruria and later a Roman colony, and the bronze Mars of Todi, an Etruscan-style statue of around 400 BCE, was found there.

tabora.s: Tabora is a city in west-central Tanzania, in the land of the Nyamwezi. It grew from the 1840s around a settlement of Arab and Swahili merchants in the chiefdom of Unyanyembe, becoming the chief inland depot of the caravan trade in ivory and slaves between the coast and Lake…

toronto.s: Toronto is the capital of the Canadian province of Ontario and Canada's largest city, on the north-west shore of Lake Ontario. Founded as York by John Graves Simcoe in 1793, it became the capital of Upper Canada and was briefly occupied by American troops in 1813.

tuva.s: Tuva is a republic of the Russian Federation in southern Siberia, on the upper Yenisei, bordering Mongolia. Inhabited mainly by Turkic-speaking Tuvans, it was part of the Qing Empire's Mongolian frontier until 1911, became a Russian protectorate in 1914 and was the nominally…

tanit.s: Tanit was the chief goddess of Carthage and the Punic world, often paired with the god Baal Hammon and called 'face of Baal'. Her emblem, a triangle topped by a horizontal bar and a disc, appears on thousands of stelae, coins and mosaics from North Africa, Sicily, Sardinia and…

takano-choei.s: Takano Chōei was a Japanese physician and scholar of Dutch learning (rangaku) who studied under Philipp Franz von Siebold at Nagasaki. In 1838 he criticised the shogunate's policy of firing on foreign ships and was imprisoned in the purge of 1839.

tejapala.s: Tejapala was a Jain minister of the Vaghela rulers of Gujarat in the 13th century, serving with his elder brother Vastupala under Viradhavala at Dholka. The brothers were famous patrons of Jain temples and of literature.

tenali.s: Tenali is a town in Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh, India, in the Krishna delta, criss-crossed by irrigation canals. In the Middle Ages the nearby village of Chandavolu was a seat of the Velanati Chodas.

treaty-of-sapienza.s: The Treaty of Sapienza was an agreement of 1209 between the Republic of Venice and Geoffrey I of Villehardouin, ruler of the Frankish Principality of Achaea in the Peloponnese. Named after the island of Sapienza off Modon, it recognised Venetian possession of the ports of…

tomb-of-the-lictor.s: The Tomb of the Lictor (Tomba del Littore) is an Etruscan circle grave of the 7th century BCE at Vetulonia in Tuscany, excavated by Isidoro Falchi in the late 19th century. Among its finds was an iron double-headed axe set in a bundle of iron rods, taken as an early example of…

terai.s: The Terai is a belt of lowland plains, marshes and forest along the foot of the Himalayas, mostly in southern Nepal and the adjoining parts of India. Once malarial and thinly settled, it was home to the Shakya and Koliya republics and to Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace.

thorigny-marble.s: The Thorigny Marble is an inscribed Roman statue base of 238 CE, found at Vieux, ancient Aregenua, in Normandy and now kept at Saint-Lô. It honours Titus Sennius Sollemnis, a leading citizen of the Viducasses, and reproduces letters from Roman governors praising him, making it…

tuluva-dynasty.s: The Tuluva dynasty was the third ruling house of the Vijayanagara Empire, founded when Vira Narasimha, son of the general Narasa Nayaka, took the throne in 1505. Under his brother Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) the empire reached its height.

theodoric-i.s: Theodoric I was king of the Visigoths from 418 to 451, ruling the federate kingdom that Rome had settled in Aquitaine, with Toulouse as its capital. He repeatedly tried to expand towards the Mediterranean coast at Roman expense, but in 451 he joined the Roman general Aetius…

tour-magne.s: The Tour Magne is a tower on Mont Cavalier, the highest point of Nîmes in southern France. A pre-Roman stone tower built by the Volcae Arecomici was enlarged under Augustus into a tall polygonal tower forming part of the Roman walls of Nemausus.

tigurini.s: The Tigurini were one of the four cantons (pagi) of the Helvetii, a Celtic people of the Swiss plateau. Joining the migration of the Cimbri, they defeated and killed the consul Lucius Cassius Longinus near Agen in 107 BCE under their leader Divico.

toulouse.s: Toulouse is a city on the Garonne in south-western France. As Tolosa it was the chief town of the Volcae Tectosages and then a Roman city; it was the capital of the Visigothic kingdom from 418 to 507 and later of the counts of Toulouse, rulers of much of Languedoc, until the…

terracina.s: Terracina is a town on the coast of Lazio, Italy, south-east of Rome, where the Via Appia reaches the sea. Called Anxur by the Volsci, it was taken by Rome and became the colony of Tarracina in 329 BCE.

traprain-law-treasure.s: The Traprain Law Treasure is a hoard of late Roman silver, more than 250 pieces of cut and crushed tableware weighing over 20 kg, found in 1919 on the hillfort of Traprain Law in East Lothian, Scotland. Buried in the early 5th century, it was probably a payment or gift to the…

tiberius-coruncanius.s: Tiberius Coruncanius was a Roman statesman and the first plebeian pontifex maximus, around 254 BCE. As consul in 280 BCE he defeated the Etruscan cities of Volsinii and Vulci and celebrated a triumph over them, before turning south against Pyrrhus.

tosora.s: Tosora is a village in Wajo Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia, near Lake Tempe, that was the capital of the Bugis kingdom of Wajo. It was the seat of the elected ruler, the Arung Matoa, and of Wajo's council of lords.

tisquantum.s: Tisquantum, better known as Squanto, was a Patuxet man who acted as interpreter and guide for the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony. Kidnapped by the English captain Thomas Hunt in 1614 and sold in Spain, he reached England and returned home in 1619 to find his people wiped out by…

tarkwa.s: Tarkwa is a mining town in the Western Region of Ghana, in the former territory of Wassa. Gold had been worked in the area for centuries before European companies opened deep mines there from the late 1870s, served from 1901 by a railway from the port of Sekondi.

timor.s: Timor is an island at the southern end of the Malay Archipelago, north of Australia, divided today between the independent state of Timor-Leste in the east and Indonesia's West Timor. Its sandalwood drew Chinese, Malay and Portuguese traders, and from the 17th century the…

tyburn.s: Tyburn was a village west of London, near today's Marble Arch, whose name became a byword for execution. From 1196 to 1783 it was the main place of public hanging for London and Middlesex, from 1571 using a large triangular gallows known as the Tyburn Tree.

treaty-of-greenville.s: The Treaty of Greenville was signed on 3 August 1795 at Fort Greenville, in present-day Ohio, between the United States and the nations of the Western Confederacy after their defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers. In return for payments in goods, the Native nations ceded most…

tong-yabghu-khagan.s: Tong Yabghu Khagan was ruler of the Western Turkic Khaganate from about 618 until his murder around 630. Under him the khaganate reached its greatest extent, collecting tribute from the Sogdian cities and Tokharistan and fighting the Sasanian Empire.

ternopil.s: Ternopil is a city in western Ukraine on the Seret River, in the historical region of Podolia. It was founded in 1540 as a fortress by the Polish commander Jan Amor Tarnowski and passed to Austria in the partitions of Poland.

torarica.s: Torarica was the capital of the English colony of Willoughbyland on the Suriname River, a small town of planters founded in the 1650s. After the Dutch conquest of 1667 the seat of government moved to Paramaribo, nearer the coast, and Torarica declined.

tadun.s: Tadun (died 207) was a chieftain of the Wuhuan, a nomadic people of the north-eastern Chinese frontier, who led the Wuhuan of Liaoxi at the end of the Eastern Han. He allied with the warlord Yuan Shao and later sheltered Yuan Shao's sons Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi.

tibetans.s: The Tibetans are a people native to the Tibetan Plateau, speaking Tibetic languages and traditionally following Tibetan Buddhism and the Bon religion. United by the Yarlung kings in the 7th century, they built the Tibetan Empire that rivalled Tang China, and later lived under…

tshiwo.s: Tshiwo was a paramount chief of the Xhosa in the late 17th century and the father of Phalo. During his rule Xhosa settlement continued westwards towards the Fish River.

tian.s: Tian, 'Heaven', is the supreme power in ancient Chinese religion and political thought. From the Zhou dynasty, which invoked it to justify overthrowing the Shang, rulers styled themselves Son of Heaven and claimed to govern by the Mandate of Heaven, which Heaven withdrew from…

temple-of-the-feathered-serpent-xochical.s: The Temple of the Feathered Serpent is the principal monument of Xochicalco in Morelos, Mexico, built in the Epiclassic period between about 650 and 900. Its sloping base is carved with great plumed serpents, seated figures and glyphs in a style that mixes central Mexican and…

toyo-queen.s: Toyo, also read Iyo, was a queen of Wa (Japan) recorded in the Chinese Records of Wei, who succeeded Queen Himiko of Yamatai in the mid-3rd century. After Himiko's death a king failed to keep order, and Toyo, a girl of thirteen from Himiko's kin, was made ruler and peace…

tarikh-i-rashidi.s: The Tarikh-i Rashidi is a Persian history written between 1541 and 1546 in Kashmir by Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat and named after Abd al-Rashid Khan of the Yarkent Khanate. It records the history of the Chagatai khans of Moghulistan and their Dughlat amirs, together with the…

treaty-of-daan.s: The Treaty of Da'an was an agreement concluded in 1911 at Da'an, north-west of Sanaa, between the Ottoman Empire and the Zaydi imam Yahya Hamid al-Din. It gave Yahya authority over the Zaydi highlands of Yemen, including the appointment of judges and the collection of…

tlapanec-people.s: The Tlapanecs, who call themselves Me'phaa, are an indigenous people of the mountains of eastern Guerrero, Mexico, speaking an Oto-Manguean language. In pre-Hispanic times the Yopes of Yopitzinco, a Tlapanec lordship near the Pacific coast, resisted conquest by the Aztec Empire.

tarbagatai-mountains.s: The Tarbagatai Mountains are a range on the border between eastern Kazakhstan and the Xinjiang region of China, between the Altai to the north-east and the Dzungarian Alatau to the south. They lay on steppe routes between Dzungaria and the Kazakh lands, and the town of Tacheng…

tiele.s: The Tiele were a confederation of Turkic-speaking tribes of the Mongolian steppe and Central Asia recorded in Chinese sources from the 5th to the 7th century, and linked to the earlier Gaoche ('High Carts'). Subject in turn to the Rouran and the Göktürks, tribes among them…

tunja.s: Tunja is the capital of the department of Boyacá in the Eastern Andes of Colombia. Founded by the Spanish in 1539 on the site of Hunza, the seat of the Muisca zaque, it became one of the main towns of the New Kingdom of Granada.

trongsa.s: Trongsa is a town in central Bhutan built around Trongsa Dzong, a seventeenth-century fortress-monastery that commands the old route between the east and west of the country. Its governors, the penlops of Trongsa, came to dominate central and eastern Bhutan, and Ugyen…

tibeto-burman-languages.s: Tibeto-Burman is the name for the large group of Sino-Tibetan languages other than Chinese, spoken from the Himalayas to Myanmar and south-western China. It includes Tibetan and Burmese, both with long literary traditions, hundreds of smaller languages, and extinct languages…

tonpa-shenrab-miwoche.s: Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche is the legendary founder of the Bon religion of Tibet. Bon tradition holds that he lived many thousands of years ago in the land of Olmo Lungring, west of Tibet, and that his teachings spread through the kingdom of Zhangzhung; his life is told in long…

thukela-river.s: The Thukela, or Tugela, is the largest river of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. It rises in the Drakensberg, plunges over the Tugela Falls and flows about 500 kilometres east to the Indian Ocean.

taiz.s: Taiz is a city in the southern highlands of Yemen, at the foot of Mount Sabir. The Ayyubids made it a base in the late twelfth century, and it became the capital of the Rasulid dynasty, whose mosques and madrasas, such as the Ashrafiyya, still stand.

thirteen-years-war-1454-1466.s: The Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466) was fought between the Kingdom of Poland, allied with the Prussian Confederation of towns and nobles, and the Teutonic Order. It began when the Prussian estates rebelled against the Order and placed themselves under King Casimir IV Jagiellon.

third-anglo-maratha-war.s: The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818) was the final conflict between the British East India Company and the Maratha Confederacy. Peshwa Baji Rao II and the rulers of Nagpur and Indore rose against the Company during its campaign against the Pindaris, but were defeated at…

third-javanese-war-of-succession.s: The Third Javanese War of Succession was fought from 1749 to 1757 in the Mataram Sultanate of Java between Pakubuwono III, supported by the Dutch East India Company, and the rebel princes Mangkubumi and Raden Mas Said. The Treaty of Giyanti (1755) divided Mataram between…

third-italian-war-of-independence.s: The Third Italian War of Independence was fought in 1866 between the Kingdom of Italy and the Austrian Empire, alongside the Austro-Prussian War. Although Italy was defeated at Custoza on land and at Lissa at sea, Prussia's victory over Austria allowed Italy to gain Venetia…

transition-from-sui-to-tang.s: The transition from Sui to Tang was the period of rebellion and civil war in China from 613 to 628, as the Sui dynasty collapsed under the burden of Emperor Yang's failed wars against Goguryeo and his great building projects. Many rival leaders fought for power; Li Yuan…

tokhtamysh-timur-war.s: The Tokhtamysh–Timur war was fought from 1386 to 1395 between Tokhtamysh, khan of the Golden Horde, and his former patron Timur. Tokhtamysh raided Timur's lands in Azerbaijan and Transoxiana, but Timur defeated him at the Kondurcha River (1391) and the Terek (1395) and then…

tonkin-campaign.s: The Tonkin campaign was the French military campaign of 1883 to 1886 to occupy Tonkin in northern Vietnam and establish a protectorate there. French forces fought Vietnamese troops, the Black Flag Army of Liu Yongfu and Chinese armies, and the campaign merged with the…

third-macedonian-war.s: The Third Macedonian War was fought from 171 to 168 BCE between Rome and King Perseus of Macedon. After early setbacks, the Roman consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus crushed the Macedonian phalanx at Pydna in June 168 BCE, and Perseus was taken to Rome.

tibet-ladakh-mughal-war.s: The Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War was fought from 1679 to 1684 between the Ganden Phodrang government of Tibet under the Fifth Dalai Lama and the kingdom of Ladakh. A Tibetan and Mongol army invaded Ladakh and besieged Basgo, and Ladakh obtained help from the Mughal governor of…

third-ottoman-venetian-war.s: The Third Ottoman–Venetian War was fought from 1537 to 1540 between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent. After an Ottoman siege of Corfu failed, a Holy League fleet under Andrea Doria was defeated by Hayreddin Barbarossa at Preveza in…

trunajaya-rebellion.s: The Trunajaya rebellion was a revolt led by the Madurese prince Trunajaya against the Mataram Sultanate in Java. Supported by Makassarese fighters, the rebels sacked the court at Plered in 1677, and Amangkurat I died in flight.

tecumsehs-war.s: Tecumseh's War was the conflict between the United States and a confederacy of Native American nations led by the Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa, who opposed land cessions in the Northwest Territory. William Henry Harrison destroyed their settlement of…

third-samnite-war.s: The Third Samnite War was fought from 298 to 290 BCE between Rome and the Samnites, who were allied with Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls. The Roman victory at Sentinum in 295 BCE broke the coalition, and Rome won again at Aquilonia in 293 BCE.

travancore-dutch-war.s: The Travancore–Dutch War was fought between the Dutch East India Company and the kingdom of Travancore under Marthanda Varma on the Malabar Coast of south-west India. Travancore defeated a Dutch force at the Battle of Colachel in 1741, one of the first defeats of a European…

tiryns.s: Tiryns is a Mycenaean archaeological site in the Argolis, in the Peloponnese of Greece, a hill fort that was at its most important between about 1400 and 1200 BCE. Its walls, usually 6 metres thick and once 9–10 metres high, with tunnels running through them, gave it the…

tres-zapotes.s: Tres Zapotes is an archaeological site at the western edge of the Los Tuxtlas mountains in Veracruz, Mexico, sometimes called the third Olmec capital, though it remained a regional centre for some 2,000 years, from perhaps 900 BCE until about 900 CE. The first colossal head to…

taruga.s: Taruga is an archaeological site of the Nok culture in central Nigeria, about 60 kilometres south-east of Abuja, known for terracotta figurines and early iron working. A trial excavation of eight days in January 1961 found the bases and walls of smelting furnaces still in…

teouma.s: Teouma is an archaeological site on the island of Efate in Vanuatu with the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands, a Lapita burial ground thought to be about 3,200 to 3,000 years old. Found in late 2003, its 26 burials held 36 individuals, with decorated red pottery;…

temple-of-the-inscriptions.s: The Temple of the Inscriptions is a stepped pyramid at Palenque in Chiapas, Mexico, built as the funerary monument of the 7th-century Maya ruler K'inich Janaab Pakal. Begun in the last decade of his life, it was completed by his son K'inich Kan Bahlam II shortly after 683.

thurgood-marshall.s: Thurgood Marshall was an American lawyer and the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, serving from 1967 to 1991. A student of Charles Hamilton Houston at Howard University, he led the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund and won 29 of…

tolpuddle-martyrs.s: The Tolpuddle Martyrs were six agricultural labourers from Tolpuddle in Dorset, England, convicted in 1834 of swearing a secret oath as members of a friendly society. Led by the Methodist local preacher George Loveless, they had formed the Friendly Society of Agricultural…

the-communist-manifesto.s: The Communist Manifesto, originally the Manifesto of the Communist Party, is a political pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, commissioned by the Communist League and published anonymously in German in London in February 1848. It argues that "the history of all hitherto…

tulsidas.s: Tulsidas was a Hindu poet-saint of 16th-century northern India, devoted to the god Rama, who spent most of his life in Varanasi and Ayodhya. A Brahmin schooled in Sanskrit and the Vedas, he is best known for the Ramcharitmanas, a retelling of the Sanskrit Ramayana in the…

tukaram.s: Tukaram was a 17th-century Marathi poet-saint of the Varkari tradition, born at Dehu in Maharashtra and devoted to the god Vithoba, a form of Vishnu. In his abhangas, devotional poems in a simple folk style, he attacked caste hierarchy, mechanical ritual and the misconduct of…

tongwen-guan.s: The Tongwen Guan, or School of Combined Learning, was a government school of Western languages and science founded at Beijing in 1862 to train interpreters for the Zongli Yamen. It opened with ten students of English; a proposal to add astronomy and mathematics was opposed by…
